network.overall_strategy: This is a connected, conditional synthesis network containing 31 chemical-species nodes, 20 reaction nodes and 10 distinct reaction sequences to glutamate. The ten pathways include experimentally distinct mineral implementations; they are not claimed to represent ten unrelated mechanisms. A carbon-growth module supplies 2-oxoglutarate for eight branches, while acrolein–cyanide chemistry and atmospheric discharge bypass it. Pyruvate, an initial glyoxylate inventory, formaldehyde, acrolein, cyanide, ammonia, hydrogen, hydroxylamine, diamidophosphate and reducing minerals are conditional external supplies; their simultaneous geological availability is not established. In particular, glyoxylate regeneration by transamination cannot supply the initial glyoxylate needed to start carbon growth. Reaction mechanisms contain explicit balanced equations, while inputs and outputs contain each ID only once. Acids and ammonia use reference protonation forms; actual aqueous speciation follows the stated pH. Mineral oxidation products and the discharge equation are identified where they provide formal bookkeeping rather than measured product distributions. Glutamate is represented by neutral glutamic acid for bookkeeping and is not assumed to be exclusively L-glutamate. All modules exclude molecular oxygen. Nonphotochemical surface modules require UV attenuation by water, sediment or mineral cover. Branch-specific conditioning, catalyst removal and concentration are requirements, not demonstrated transport processes. No complete, quantitatively closed geological synthesis is claimed. N-acyl, thermal-mixture and impact branches are omitted rather than implying that unresolved hydrolysis or extreme-event chemistry constitutes an established continuous source of free glutamate. Under the restricted role vocabulary, intermediate also covers terminal coproducts; null formation environments indicate external or multiple possible origins.

molecules.common_name: Ammonia; reference form of the ammonia/ammonium pool
Glyoxylic acid; initially externally supplied and subsequently regenerable
Ferrous ion; reference form of oxidized iron inventory
Hydrogen cyanide; reference form of the HCN/cyanide pool

reactions.name: Hydrogen-driven carbon growth to 2-oxoglutarate, represented as a lumped reductive-aldol channel
agents: Metallic nickel on silica–alumina: hydrogen-activation catalyst

conditions.other: Anoxic, approximately pH 8. A proposed implementation uses 10-30 mM pyruvate and an externally supplied glyoxylate inventory. These precursor concentrations are a scenario, not a reported optimum or yield. Retain the nickel-containing suspension for rxn_002, or recover the ketoacid fraction before chemically incompatible branches.

reactions.mechanism: Balanced selected-channel equation: pyruvic acid + glyoxylic acid + H2 -> 2-oxoglutaric acid + H2O. Aldol carbon-carbon bond formation followed by dehydration and hydrogenation provides a chemically coherent net route. This node coarse-grains carbon growth and does not assert a resolved elementary mechanism.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) support H2/Ni-driven reductive-aldol carbon growth alongside amino-acid formation. Muchowska et al. (2019) independently establish access to 2-oxoglutarate in pyruvate/glyoxylate networks. The precise flux through the selected net channel and its productivity in an unpurified environmental mixture remain conditional; the proposed concatenation is not an end-to-end geological demonstration. Competing carbonyl hydrogenation, substrate dilution and ketoacid destruction must be measured. No yield from a downstream commercial-ketoacid experiment is assigned to this upstream node.

reactions.name: Nickel-catalyzed hydrogen reductive amination
agents: Metallic nickel on silica–alumina: activates H2 and mediates imine reduction

conditions.other: Approximately 30 mM ketoacid, ammonium bicarbonate medium, pH 8, 72 h, anoxic. The 6-150 mM ammonium range reported across the study is not a glutamate-specific optimum. The carbon-growth mixture can be evaluated without an obligatory environmental transfer.

reactions.mechanism: Balanced equation: 2-oxoglutaric acid + NH3 + H2 -> glutamic acid + H2O. Reversible imine/iminium formation is followed by hydrogenation at the nickel surface.
reactions.reasoning: Glutamate formation under these conditions is supported by Kaur et al. (2024). Nickel is a catalyst and H2 is the consumed reductant. The reported 6-84% combined amino-acid-plus-hydroxyacid range concerns a substrate panel, not glutamate alone. Direct reduction to hydroxyglutarate competes. Mayer and Moran (2022) show that 2-oxoglutarate imine formation and reductive amination are comparatively unfavorable, explaining the dependence on ammonia activity and surface reduction kinetics.

reactions.name: Meteoritic Fe/Ni-catalyzed hydrogen reductive amination
agents: Finely ground Aletai meteorite: experimentally tested Fe/Ni-rich heterogeneous catalyst

conditions.other: Approximately 30 mM ketoacid, ammonium bicarbonate, pH 8, 72 h, anoxic. For this alternative catalyst test, use recovered 2-oxoglutarate-containing solution without residual supported nickel; equivalent natural substrate delivery is not demonstrated.

reactions.mechanism: Balanced equation: 2-oxoglutaric acid + NH3 + H2 -> glutamic acid + H2O. Meteorite metal surfaces activate hydrogen and reduce the ammonia-derived imine.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) directly support the meteorite-catalyzed conversion. This is a distinct material implementation of reductive amination, not a new bond-forming mechanism. Its inclusion is justified by the experimentally demonstrated substitution of naturally occurring Fe/Ni-rich material for a manufactured catalyst. Competing hydroxyacid production and the need for concentrated ketoacid remain. The meteorite experiment does not establish the efficiency of the upstream carbon-growth module on the same material.

reactions.name: Ferrous-hydroxide-mediated reductive amination
agents: Fresh iron(II) hydroxide: consumed reducing solid, not a turnover catalyst

conditions.pressure: Closed aqueous vessel; pressure sufficient to retain liquid water
conditions.other: Proposed pH 8-9.5, millimolar ketoacid, substantial ammonia/ammonium excess and freshly prepared Fe(OH)2. The supplied report does not give a separate optimized Fe(OH)2 temperature, loading or glutamate yield. These conditions are not represented as a replication of its FeS optimum.

reactions.mechanism: Balanced formal redox equation: 2-oxoglutaric acid + NH3 + 2 Fe(OH)2 + H2O -> glutamic acid + 2 Fe(OH)3. Two Fe(II) oxidation equivalents reduce the imine. Fe(OH)3 represents a hydrated Fe(III) oxidation inventory, not an experimentally established crystalline product.
reactions.reasoning: Huber and Wächtershäuser (2003) report reductive amination with freshly prepared Fe(OH)2 as well as FeS. Their 35% maximum glutamate yield and approximately 20-equivalent mineral loading specifically concern FeS and must not be transferred to this hydroxide branch. The reaction family is experimentally supported, but the numerical environmental window and ferric-product representation here are conditional. Freshness, mineral passivation, ammonia concentration and the actual iron oxidation products require verification.

reactions.name: Reductive amination on partially electroreduced FeS
agents: Partially electroreduced FeS: preconditioned redox-active mineral surface

conditions.pressure: Approximately ambient pressure during the aqueous conversion
conditions.other: Approximately 5 mM 2-oxoglutarate, pH 9.6, large ammonium excess of roughly 0.5 M, 48 h, anoxic. The laboratory mineral was preconditioned near -0.7 V versus SHE for seven days. That preparation is a conditional external mineral supply, not an autonomous activation step demonstrated here.

reactions.mechanism: Balanced reference redox equation: 2-oxoglutaric acid + NH3 + Fe + 2 H+ -> glutamic acid + H2O + Fe2+. The Fe(0)/Fe(II) pair represents two-electron reducing inventory within the preconditioned mineral system; it does not identify the unique active surface phase or prove release of freely dissolved Fe2+ at alkaline pH.
reactions.reasoning: Kitadai et al. (2019) report nearly complete 2-oxoglutarate conversion under the cited alkaline conditions. The formal iron equation is a bookkeeping model, whereas the reported substrate conversion is experimental evidence. Natural production and replenishment of the strongly reduced surface remain unresolved. Calling the material a freely regenerating catalyst would be unjustified. The cool interface is labeled Biochemical rather than assigning room-temperature data to a 350-600 K vent.

reactions.name: ZnS-photocatalyzed reductive amination with sulfite

conditions.other: Anoxic illuminated suspension, pH approximately 9, large ammonium excess, sulfite hole scavenger, approximately 4 h irradiation. Use a shallow illuminated interface; deep hydrothermal placement is excluded. Remove upstream nickel and evaluate residual organic photochemistry before concatenation.

reactions.mechanism: Balanced two-electron endpoint equation: 2-oxoglutaric acid + NH3 + SO3^2- -> glutamic acid + SO4^2-. Photoexcited ZnS supplies conduction-band electrons to an imine, while sulfite consumes photogenerated holes. Sulfate is the formal fully oxidized sulfur endpoint, not a claim that all sulfur products were identified.
reactions.reasoning: Wang et al. (2012) report approximately 0.5% glutamate after four hours without sulfite and an approximately sixfold enhancement with sulfite. Light-only and dark-ZnS controls did not give the relevant conversion. Molecular oxygen is not required for the written electron balance. Sulfur-radical side products, catalyst stability, UV degradation and the low glutamate yield limit environmental extrapolation.

reactions.name: 2-Oxoglutarate oxime formation

conditions.other: Anoxic aqueous ketoacid mixture followed by hydroxylamine addition. A pH 4-7 screening window is proposed; it is not an independently reported glutamate-specific optimum. Initial hydroxylamine supply is conditional.

reactions.mechanism: Balanced equation: 2-oxoglutaric acid + NH2OH -> 2-oxoglutarate oxime + H2O. Hydroxylamine adds to the keto carbonyl and the adduct dehydrates.
reactions.reasoning: Muchowska et al. (2019) support ketoacid-to-oxime chemistry within their iron-promoted network and subsequent amino-acid formation after hydroxylamine/Fe(0) addition. The present upstream H2/Ni module is not the same experiment, so combining it with this branch requires compatibility testing. Kitadai et al. (2019) identify uncertain Hadean hydroxylamine availability as a substantive limitation.

reactions.name: Zero-valent-iron reduction of the oxime to glutamate
agents: Zero-valent iron: consumed four-electron reducing inventory

conditions.other: Anoxic heated suspension after oxime formation; proposed mildly acidic-to-near-neutral medium. At least two formal Fe(0)-to-Fe(II) equivalents are required per oxime; actual mineral excess may be larger because corrosion and side reductions consume metal.

reactions.mechanism: Balanced equation: 2-oxoglutarate oxime + 2 Fe + 4 H+ -> glutamic acid + H2O + 2 Fe2+. Reduction removes the N-O functionality and reduces the C=N bond. H+ denotes proton equivalents supplied by the aqueous buffer, not a requirement for a concentrated free-proton solution.
reactions.reasoning: Muchowska et al. (2019) experimentally support glutamate formation from ketoacids using hydroxylamine and Fe(0), with oxime intermediates implicated. The four-electron equation explicitly accounts for metal consumption. The reported integration advantage applies to their Fe-promoted carbon network; it does not establish unchanged efficiency after the separate nickel module used here.

reactions.name: Formaldehyde Strecker synthesis of aminoacetonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed ammonia-rich, anoxic pond concentrate at pH 8-9.5, with 10-100 mM carbonyl and sufficient cyanide. These concentrations are a network scenario, not an optimized experiment in the supplied report. Attenuate UV and limit loss of volatile HCN and ammonia.

reactions.mechanism: Balanced equation: formaldehyde + NH3 + HCN -> aminoacetonitrile + H2O. Carbonyl-ammonia condensation followed by cyanide capture gives the glycine aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This is standard Strecker chemistry, but the specific formaldehyde preparation and operating window are not documented by an experiment in the supplied report; this upstream implementation is therefore explicitly speculative relative to the supplied evidence. Van Trump and Miller (1972) support the broader Strecker framework, and Pulletikurti et al. (2022) establish aminoacetonitrile as a relevant nitrogen donor in related chemistry. No yield is assigned.

reactions.name: Aminoacetonitrile hydrolysis to glycine
agents: Aqueous acid: nitrile and amide hydrolysis promoter

conditions.other: Proposed pH 1-2, sustained liquid water and days-to-weeks heating in a locally acidic geothermal reservoir. The residence-time range is a scenario rather than a reported endpoint. Remove or deplete residual cyanide, then adjust the recovered glycine solution to pH approximately 5 before Al(III)-assisted transamination.

reactions.mechanism: Balanced equation: aminoacetonitrile + 2 H2O -> glycine + NH3. Sequential nitrile hydration and amide hydrolysis release glycine; protonation changes are absorbed into the reference-species convention.
reactions.reasoning: The transformation is conventional aminonitrile hydrolysis, but the supplied report does not validate this particular glycine-release protocol; its rate and environmental realization are explicitly speculative. The nitrile-hydrolysis bottleneck is consistent with the limitations discussed for Van Trump and Miller (1972) and Fernández-García et al. (2017). Glycine must actually be accumulated and separated from residual cyanide before rxn_011; the subsequent 44% transamination result does not validate this upstream step.

reactions.name: Aluminum-assisted transamination from glycine
agents: Soluble Al(III) salt: Lewis-acid transamination promoter

conditions.catalyst: Al(III), for example potassium aluminum sulfate
conditions.other: Concentrated aqueous substrates, approximately pH 5. Related experiments used 0.2 M 2-oxoglutarate and 44 h incubation. Recover and concentrate ketoacid and glycine fractions separately; remove residual cyanide and nickel before combining. Soluble Al(III) must remain available rather than precipitating with phosphate.

reactions.mechanism: Balanced equation: 2-oxoglutaric acid + glycine -> glutamic acid + glyoxylic acid. Metal-assisted imine exchange transfers reduced nitrogen without an external reductant.
reactions.reasoning: Stubbs et al. (2020) report 44% glutamate in hot acidic Al(III)-assisted transamination. Pulletikurti et al. (2022) support related approximately 0.2 M, pH 5, 80 C experiments. Evaporation is a possible concentration mechanism, not a demonstrated source of these simultaneous concentrations. Regenerated glyoxylate could support further carbon growth only after suitable pH and catalyst conditioning; this is not a demonstrated self-sustaining cycle.

reactions.name: Diamidophosphate hydrolysis supplying ammonia

conditions.temperature: Approximately 300 K during hydantoin formation; up to 353 K during later hydrolysis
conditions.other: Concentrated bicarbonate-buffered medium, pH 8.5; the cited formulation supplied approximately 0.7 M DAP. Ammonia release can overlap hydantoin formation. Complete DAP hydrolysis before rxn_013 is neither required nor experimentally established.

reactions.mechanism: Balanced complete-hydrolysis equation in acid reference forms: H5N2O2P + 2 H2O -> H3PO4 + 2 NH3. Sequential P-N bond hydrolysis passes through partially hydrolyzed phosphorus species, which this supply node coarse-grains.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) use DAP as an ammonia-providing reagent in the high-yield hydantoin formulation. The equation is the balanced hydrolysis endpoint, not a measured time-resolved ammonia-release curve. Its rate must be compatible with rxn_013, and the prebiotic supply of 0.7 M DAP remains a major condition. Phosphate-rich solutions are kept separate from the Al(III) branch because precipitation could disable its promoter.

reactions.name: Decarboxylative Bucherer-Bergs formation of the glutamate hydantoin

conditions.other: Approximately 0.35 M 2-oxoglutarate, 0.42 M cyanide, 0.7 M DAP ammonia source, 0.5 M bicarbonate, pH 8.5, 21 days. DAP release is represented by rxn_012. A concentrated, buffered, UV-screened reservoir is required; natural co-concentration is not demonstrated.

reactions.mechanism: Balanced unlabeled net equation: 2-oxoglutaric acid + HCN + NH3 -> 5-(2-carboxyethyl)hydantoin + H2O. Cyanide addition, nitrogen incorporation, carbamylation, cyclization and decarboxylation produce the protected amino-acid precursor. Inorganic-carbon uptake and CO2 release cancel from this net representation; the equation is not an isotopic atom map.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) report approximately 96% hydantoin under these highly concentrated, multiweek conditions. Cyanide and DAP are reagents, not catalysts. The yield concerns protected hydantoin, not free glutamate. This branch requires concentrating and conditioning the upstream ketoacid solution by more than an order of magnitude; no natural concentrating sequence accomplishing the entire formulation has been demonstrated.

reactions.name: Hydantoin ring opening to N-carbamoylglutamate

conditions.other: Heat the concentrated hydantoin-forming mixture for up to 14 days, initially near pH 8.5, while retaining liquid water. This and rxn_015 share the reported hydrolysis interval; separate reaction-specific rates are not available.

reactions.mechanism: Balanced equation: 5-(2-carboxyethyl)hydantoin + H2O -> N-carbamoylglutamic acid. Hydrolytic ring opening exposes the amino-acid carboxyl group while retaining N-carbamoyl protection.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) support hydrolysis through carbamoylated intermediates. Their endpoint of approximately 19% glutamate with 72% hydantoin remaining after 14 days at 80 C constrains the combined hydrolysis sequence, not this individual rate. The N-carbamoyl node makes the protected/free-target distinction explicit; its separate yield is not invented.

reactions.name: Decarbamoylation releasing free glutamate

conditions.other: Same prolonged aqueous heating interval as rxn_014; initially approximately pH 8.5. Monitor pH and retention of ammonia and inorganic carbon. No separate completion time or quantitative conversion is assigned.

reactions.mechanism: Balanced equation: N-carbamoylglutamic acid + H2O -> glutamic acid + NH3 + CO2. Hydrolysis of the carbamoyl substituent and carbamic-acid decomposition liberate the amino group.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) confirm free glutamate by NMR spiking after the complete hydantoin/hydrolysis sequence. Approximately 19% glutamate after 14 days is the relevant target yield, rather than the 96% protected-intermediate yield. The individual contributions of ring opening and decarbamoylation to the bottleneck are unresolved.

reactions.name: Conjugate cyanide addition to acrolein

conditions.other: Approximately pH 9.2. The modern combined addition/cyanohydrin experiment used approximately 140 mM acrolein and 700 mM KCN. The free aldehyde is an exchanging intermediate, not assumed to accumulate quantitatively.

reactions.mechanism: Balanced equation: acrolein + HCN -> 3-cyanopropanal. Conjugate cyanide addition across the activated carbon-carbon double bond installs the future terminal-carboxyl carbon.
reactions.reasoning: Van Trump and Miller (1972) propose acrolein-centered chemistry relevant to glutamate. Fernández-García et al. (2017), as summarized in the supplied report, support the addition/cyanohydrin reservoir with approximately 95% yield under concentrated conditions. That number is not a separate free-3-cyanopropanal yield and is not a glutamate yield. Acrolein polymerization and cyanide availability compete with the desired route.

reactions.name: Capture of the cyanopropanal cyanohydrin reservoir

conditions.other: Same aqueous cyanide-rich medium as rxn_016, approximately pH 9.2. The approximately 95% reported reservoir yield applies to the combined acrolein/cyanide chemistry rather than to two independently quantified steps.

reactions.mechanism: Balanced equation: 3-cyanopropanal + HCN -> 2-hydroxypentanedinitrile. Reversible 1,2-addition at the aldehyde stores the C5 framework as a cyanohydrin.
reactions.reasoning: Fernández-García et al. (2017) support the cyanohydrin reservoir identified in the supplied research. This intermediate helps explain accumulation under cyanide excess, but its stability can oppose subsequent ammonia incorporation. Treating it as automatically equivalent to an aminonitrile would conceal a real mechanistic bottleneck.

reactions.name: Ammonia-driven conversion of the cyanohydrin reservoir to the glutamate aminodinitrile

conditions.other: Proposed pH 8.5-9.5 and 0.1-1 M total ammonia/ammonium. Adjust ammonia-to-cyanide activity after reservoir formation, retain volatile reagents and attenuate destructive UV. These are exploratory conditions, not a reported optimized glutamate-precursor protocol.

reactions.mechanism: Balanced net equation: 2-hydroxypentanedinitrile + NH3 -> 2-aminopentanedinitrile + H2O. Reversible cyanohydrin dissociation exposes the aldehyde, ammonia forms an imine, and cyanide capture gives the aminodinitrile. Direct substitution of an unactivated hydroxyl group is not assumed.
reactions.reasoning: The sequence follows the acrolein/Strecker proposal of Van Trump and Miller (1972) and the reservoir chemistry of Fernández-García et al. (2017). The supplied evidence does not establish a quantitative yield for this exact reservoir-to-aminodinitrile conversion; this link and its operating window are explicitly speculative. Excess cyanide can favor the cyanohydrin rather than the imine, so high intermediate yield alone does not establish pathway throughput.

reactions.name: Exhaustive aminodinitrile hydrolysis to free glutamate
agents: Aqueous acid: nitrile and amide hydrolysis promoter

conditions.other: Proposed locally acidic pH 1-2 reservoir, sustained water availability and days-to-weeks residence, potentially longer. Cyanide depletion and acidification must precede hydrolysis. The proposed duration is not an experimentally established completion time for this substrate.

reactions.mechanism: Balanced equation: 2-aminopentanedinitrile + 4 H2O -> glutamic acid + 2 NH3. Both nitriles must undergo hydration and subsequent amide hydrolysis; partial hydrolysis does not constitute free-glutamate production.
reactions.reasoning: Van Trump and Miller (1972) motivate the glutamate-forming Strecker framework, and Fernández-García et al. (2017) support upstream nitrile chemistry. Complete hydrolysis of this specific precursor under the proposed mild geological window is not quantified in the supplied evidence and is explicitly conditional. Amide-containing products, including glutamine-level products, may persist. Free glutamate must be measured independently rather than inferred from loss of the aminodinitrile.

reactions.name: Reducing-atmosphere electrical-discharge reachability of glutamate

conditions.temperature: Approximately 300-330 K bulk aqueous collection phase; nonthermal discharge chemistry is not assigned this temperature
conditions.other: Repeated electrical discharge through an anoxic CH4/N2 atmosphere over water containing trace ammonia, followed by aqueous collection and analytical recovery. Exact gas partial pressures, exposure duration and work-up details are not specified in the supplied report and are not invented here. Any analytical hydrolysis must be distinguished from pre-existing free glutamate.

reactions.mechanism: Atom-balanced reachability envelope: 20 CH4 + N2 + 2 NH3 + 16 H2O -> 4 glutamic acid + 41 H2. Electrical activation produces a complex C/N reaction mixture that can reach glutamate. This equation demonstrates elemental conservation only: its coefficients are not gas-mixture proportions, measured H2 yields, nitrogen-source assignments or a selective overall experimental reaction.
reactions.reasoning: Ring et al. (1972) identify glutamic acid in discharge products by ion-exchange chromatography and GC-MS. Schlesinger and Miller (1983) show that strongly reducing mixtures favor diverse amino acids, whereas CO2 without H2 gives extremely low yields dominated by glycine. The node is therefore an experimentally supported reachability channel with unresolved internal chemistry, not a quantitatively predictive reactor model. It avoids assigning unidentified polymeric mixtures a fictitious molecular formula and explicitly balances every represented element.

pathways.name: Hydrogen/nickel carbon growth followed by hydrogen/nickel amination
pathways.description: Externally supplied pyruvate and initial glyoxylate enter a reductive carbon-growth module, followed by ammonia-dependent hydrogenation on nickel. This pathway minimizes obligatory catalyst changes, although the selected upstream flux and overall yield remain unclosed.

pathways.name: Carbon growth followed by meteoritic-metal hydrogenation
pathways.description: The recovered ketoacid fraction is converted using an experimentally demonstrated natural Fe/Ni-rich catalyst. This is a distinct catalyst pathway, not an independent reductive-amination mechanism; carbon growth on the meteorite itself is not assumed.

pathways.name: Ferrous-hydroxide reducing-solid pathway
pathways.description: Carbon-grown 2-oxoglutarate is aminated using fresh Fe(OH)2 as a consumed electron source. The mineral family is supported experimentally, while the proposed environmental operating window and ferric oxidation inventory require verification.

pathways.name: Preconditioned reduced-FeS interface pathway
pathways.description: Recovered 2-oxoglutarate is exposed to strongly reduced FeS-associated surfaces under the mild alkaline conditions of the high-conversion experiment. The laboratory electrochemical pretreatment is an explicit external requirement, not a solved geological supply mechanism.

pathways.name: Illuminated ZnS/sulfite pathway
pathways.description: The ketoacid fraction is conditioned for an illuminated, alkaline ZnS suspension with sulfite. The branch consumes a sacrificial electron donor and has a low experimentally measured target yield.

pathways.name: Hydroxylamine capture and iron reduction
pathways.description: 2-Oxoglutarate is converted to an oxime and then reduced with Fe(0). The oxime route is experimentally supported, but the present upstream nickel module is not the integrated iron-carbon experiment of Muchowska et al.; hydroxylamine supply and mixture compatibility remain conditional.

pathways.name: Strecker-derived glycine followed by transamination
pathways.description: A separate formaldehyde/cyanide/ammonia branch supplies glycine. After nitrile hydrolysis, cyanide removal, concentration and pH adjustment, glycine transfers nitrogen to 2-oxoglutarate under Al(III)-assisted conditions. Glyoxylate is regenerated, but an externally supplied glyoxylate seed is still required.

pathways.name: DAP-supported Bucherer-Bergs synthesis and protected-intermediate hydrolysis
pathways.description: Concentrated 2-oxoglutarate reacts with cyanide and DAP-derived ammonia to form a hydantoin. Ring opening and decarbamoylation release free glutamate only slowly. The reported approximately 96% hydantoin and 19% glutamate yields describe different stages and are not conflated.

pathways.name: Acrolein–cyanide route bypassing 2-oxoglutarate
pathways.description: Cyanide conjugate addition and cyanohydrin capture assemble the C5 framework from acrolein. Proposed ammonia-driven Strecker conversion produces an aminodinitrile, whose two nitriles must both be fully hydrolyzed. The reservoir is well supported; downstream throughput and environmentally effective complete hydrolysis are not established quantitatively.

pathways.name: Electrical-discharge access from simple atmospheric feedstocks
pathways.description: Reducing CH4/N2/water/trace-ammonia discharge chemistry provides experimentally demonstrated access to glutamate-containing products without a supplied multicarbon precursor. The balanced envelope is deliberately coarse-grained and cannot establish selectivity, free-product release before work-up or continuous planetary productivity.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The strongest conditional pathway. Kaur et al. (2024) support H2/Ni reductive amination and compatible reductive-aldol carbon growth. Both submitted reactions are balanced. However, rxn_001 is a lumped channel without specified intermediates, measured 2-oxoglutarate productivity or competing-product accounting. The reaction entries do not establish the experimental operating conditions. Initial glyoxylate is correctly identified as an external requirement rather than assumed to arise from subsequent regeneration.
suggestions: Specify the aldol, dehydration and hydrogenation sequence underlying rxn_001 and document 2-oxoglutarate formation in the actual reaction mixture.
Attach reaction-level conditions and citations; relevant Kaur benchmarks include 5 bar H2, pH 8, 22 degrees C and 72 hours.
Measure free-glutamate production from the stated pyruvate/glyoxylate inputs, including competing ketoacid and hydroxyacid formation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024) directly support glutamate formation using ground Aletai meteorite under H2. This establishes the downstream conversion, but does not establish equivalent activity for arbitrary meteoritic material or demonstrate conversion of the submitted carbon-growth mixture. Both reactions are balanced. Catalyst composition, accessible metal surface, loading and substrate delivery remain unspecified. The published substrate-panel yield ranges must not be treated as glutamate-specific yields.
suggestions: Specify the meteoritic material, particle size, active Fe/Ni phases and catalyst loading.
Test the carbon-growth mixture directly or document any required separation before meteoritic hydrogenation.
Report glutamate-specific yield and amino-acid versus hydroxyacid selectivity under the selected conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Huber and Wachtershauser (2003) support ferrous-hydroxide-mediated ketoacid amination. The deterministic check confirms rxn_004 is balanceable using two Fe(OH)2 and two formal ferric-product units. Treating the mineral as a consumed reductant is appropriate. However, Fe(OH)3 is bookkeeping rather than an established product distribution, and the cited 35% glutamate result belongs to the FeS implementation, not automatically this Fe(OH)2 branch. Solid freshness, loading and branch-specific operating conditions are missing.
suggestions: Provide Fe(OH)2-specific conditions and glutamate measurements rather than transferring the FeS yield.
Specify fresh-solid preparation, reducing capacity, ammonium concentration and passivation controls.
Characterize iron oxidation products and demonstrate that the delivered carbon-growth mixture remains reactive.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kitadai et al. (2019) strongly support glutamate formation on partially electroreduced FeS. The submitted Fe0/Fe2+ equation is balanceable, but is only a formal electron inventory and does not identify the active reduced-FeS material. Laboratory preconditioning near -0.7 V versus SHE for seven days is a substantive requirement, not an ordinary property of FeS. The mol_013 formula/InChI inconsistency additionally compromises species encoding without making rxn_005 a second conservation violation.
suggestions: Describe the reduced-FeS phase, preparation, loading and accessible reducing equivalents explicitly.
Specify the alkaline, room-temperature reaction conditions and ammonium inventory used for the claimed conversion.
Encode mol_013 unambiguously as iron(II), synchronize its formula and InChI, and rerun validation.
Provide a supported mineral-preconditioning scenario or retain the preconditioned material explicitly as a conditional external supply.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Wang et al. (2012) support illuminated-ZnS reductive amination, including sulfite enhancement. The net equation is balanced and does not require molecular oxygen. Experimental glutamate yields of approximately 0.5%, rising roughly sixfold with sulfite, establish target formation but not substantial accumulation in this network. Irradiation, ZnS properties, pH and substrate concentrations are unspecified. Transfer from the H2/Ni module requires demonstrated compatibility; sulfate remains a formal rather than measured exclusive oxidation endpoint.
suggestions: Specify absorbed wavelengths, photon flux, ZnS loading, sulfite concentration and the approximately pH 9 operating regime.
Demonstrate activity with the delivered upstream mixture, including any necessary metal removal or pressure adjustment.
Measure sulfite oxidation products, ZnS stability and net free-glutamate accumulation under illumination.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Muchowska, Varma and Moran (2019) support oxime formation followed by Fe0 reduction to glutamate. The four-electron reduction is correctly balanceable with two Fe atoms and four protons. Their integrated carbon-growth demonstration used Fe-promoted chemistry, however, and does not itself establish compatibility with this network's H2/Ni upstream module. Hydroxylamine supply is appropriately conditional. The mol_013 encoding inconsistency and unspecified reaction pH, temperature and iron passivation remain concerns.
suggestions: Correct mol_013 and retain the explicit two-Fe stoichiometry for oxime reduction.
Specify oxime formation and reduction conditions, distinguishing proton bookkeeping from actual aqueous pH.
Test hydroxylamine capture and Fe0 reduction in the upstream mixture, including competing oxime formation from other carbonyl compounds.
Document hydroxylamine concentration and persistence without assuming its geological supply has been established.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The Strecker-to-glycine sequence and subsequent amino-group transfer are chemically coherent. Stubbs et al. (2020), with related evidence from Pulletikurti et al. (2022), support Al(III)-assisted glutamate formation under concentrated, hot acidic conditions. All steps conserve atoms with the supplied hydrolysis coefficients. The principal gap is achieving nitrile hydrolysis and then the necessary glycine/2-oxoglutarate concentrations and available Al(III) in the actual carried-over mixture. Initial glyoxylate is correctly not supplied by its own downstream regeneration.
suggestions: Specify aminoacetonitrile hydrolysis conditions and verify glycine formation rather than assuming ambient-water hydrolysis.
Provide the transamination pH, temperature, Al(III) loading and substrate concentrations; relevant experiments used hot acidic solutions and approximately 0.2 M 2-oxoglutarate.
Demonstrate concentration, acidification and carryover compatibility between the Strecker and transamination modules.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) directly support the hydantoin route and eventual free glutamate. The supplied equations are balanced or balanceable; rxn_013 should not be labeled unbalanced merely because its net equation hides decarboxylation and CO2 exchange. Nevertheless, bicarbonate participation and ammonia-release kinetics are unspecified. The distinction between hydantoin formation and free-glutamate release is essential: the cited experiment gave 96% hydantoin, but only 19% glutamate after a further 14 days at 80 degrees C, with 72% hydantoin remaining.
suggestions: Specify the bicarbonate reservoir and explain the decarboxylation/carbamoylation sequence underlying the balanced rxn_013 net equation.
Measure DAP-mediated ammonia delivery rather than assuming instantaneous complete hydrolysis.
Provide a supported concentration and retention scenario for the approximately 0.35 M 2-oxoglutarate, concentrated cyanide/DAP and multiweek treatment.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a coherent 2-oxoglutarate-independent carbon-skeleton route, and all four reactions are balanced or balanceable. Van Trump and Miller (1972) support the route concept; Fernandez-Garcia et al. (2017) strongly support the cyanopropanal-derived cyanohydrin reservoir. Those findings do not equally establish the complete submitted sequence to free glutamate. Reaction rxn_018 needs aldehyde/imine equilibration and Strecker chemistry rather than an assumed direct OH displacement. Reaction rxn_019 must hydrolyze both nitriles beyond amide intermediates under demonstrated conditions.
suggestions: Specify cyanohydrin reversibility, imine formation and cyanide capture in rxn_018, and measure the aminodinitrile yield.
Provide conditions comparable to the reservoir experiment or justify departures from its 140 mM acrolein, 700 mM cyanide and pH 9.2.
Demonstrate exhaustive hydrolysis with separate measurements of residual nitriles, amides, cyclic products and free glutamate.
Explain reagent retention and the transition from cyanide chemistry to hydrolysis without assuming quantitative recovery.

Atmospheric composition, discharge conditions and product-mixture accounting are also unspecified.

Audit the hinted NH3 coproduct and CO2/CO inputs against the actual experiment rather than adding species solely to force balance.

evaluation.network_feedback: Not approved at the required overall-confidence threshold of 0.90. The 31-species, 20-reaction graph has sufficient nodes and is connected, with appropriate distinction between external inventories, regenerated intermediates and terminal coproducts. According to the required deterministic check, 19 reactions conserve atoms and charge as written or with coefficients; rxn_004, rxn_005, rxn_008, rxn_010, rxn_012 and rxn_019 are coefficient-adjustable, not conservation failures. Reaction rxn_020 is the sole reported conservation violation and must be corrected; the checker hints at NH3/H2 coproduct accounting and possible CO2/CO inputs. The mol_013 formula/InChI mismatch must also be repaired, especially for rxn_005 and rxn_008, without reclassifying those checked reactions as unbalanced. Several complete conditional routes have credible chemistry and experimentally supported free-glutamate-forming steps. P1 has the strongest integration support because carbon growth and reductive amination have evidence under a compatible operating window. However, the submitted reaction entries lack numerical environmental conditions, detailed mechanisms and reaction-level citations; the separate literature supports these assignments but does not establish that its conditions are implemented here. The common carbon-growth channel remains lumped, and concentration, mineral preparation, carryover compatibility and free-product accumulation are not quantitatively demonstrated. The explicit acknowledgment of conditional supplies, initial glyoxylate requirements, mineral consumption and hydrolysis limitations is scientifically appropriate. Alternative branches need not operate simultaneously or share one reservoir, and no penalty is applied for their number, feedstock identities or unspecified stereochemistry. The remaining limitation is evidential and operational: a supported collection of connected chemical possibilities has not yet been established as a comparably reliable complete synthesis network.
